publications.title: P&C Insurance core transformation:  Beyond the first wave
publications.publishedAt: PricewaterhouseCoopers - Top Insurance Industry Issues in 2017 · Jan 9, 2017
publications.description:
Core system transformations continue to be a top priority for insurers - regardless of size and product mix - in the coming year.  Three major trends emerging that go beyond the first wave of core transformation

1) Digital Transformation and Analytics- Carriers have more ambitious visions for how these programs should drive growth strategies and are no longer satisfied with simply implementing a new platform then searching for ways to achieve benefits in the post-implementation environment

2) Greenfield and Cloud-  Carriers are looking at alternate delivery approaches that align with their broader organizational visions. Some of them have recently started to explore the business and architectural simplicity of greenfield and Cloud delivery scenarios

3) Specialty and E&S- The next wave of transformation will impact specialty line carriers, which includes non-admitted (E&S), Bermuda, and London Market carriers

publications.title: Gateways to growth: Insurance portals that deliver
publications.description: Portals offer property and casualty insurers the opportunity to forge stronger agent ties and deepen policyholder relationships. But many insurers treat their portal implementation as a one-size-fits-all solution, producing results that are far short of extraordinary. We’ve identified three steps that can help insurers create portals that deliver the right results for policyholders, agents, and employees—and help promote the brand identity they want.

publications.publishedAt: PricewaterhouseCoopers - Top Insurance Industry Issues in 2014 · Jan 31, 2014
publications.description: Our observations and experience suggest that PAS transformations will continue to be a top priority for insurers – regardless of size and product mix – in 2014.  Most PAS transformations do not achieve many of their goals. However, there are several distinct ways to improve results.

publications.title: Breaking Down the Core Capabilities of a Successful PAS Transformation
publications.description: The traditional measure of success for a PAS transformation is delivering scope on time and within budget. In today’s market, this presents a challenge to carriers that continue to cling to legacy development processes.  Leading carriers focus on five core delivery capabilities, moving them beyond the status quo and differentiating themselves by using faster, more flexible approaches to policy administration transformations.

publications.title: 10 Steps to Attaining PAS Transformation Success
publications.description: Small- to mid-size insurers are investing in PAS transformations more than ever, but most of them have yet to experience the growth in core business and delivery capabilities that they're looking for.

publications.title: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication: How life insurers can streamline incentive compensation for their producers
publications.description:
The complex web of compensation schedules that has evolved over time is reaching a critical mass. The demand for simplicity and transparency in producer compensation is arising from demographic, industry, and regulatory factors.

We have observed carriers struggling with a proliferation of schedules and incentives that are not aligned with strategy, while leading carriers are establishing the flexibility to craft compensation that aligns with corporate goals. Once this flexibility is established, carriers are better able to distinguish themselves from competitors in agents’ eyes. In our view, carriers should reduce the overall number of plans offered before replacing the underlying systems supporting incentive compensation. Without simplification before system transformation, carriers will re-platform legacy problems and miss out on many possible benefits.

publications.title: Eyes on the Prize: Implementing fast, flexible policy administration systems in the P&C insurance sector
publications.description:
Insurance carriers are making an unprecedented investment in modernizing their policy administration systems and processes. The ability to successfully deliver these policy administration transformation programs will differentiate the winners from the losers and alter the competitive landscape.

PwC's Policy Administration Delivery Framework can help carriers that are seeking to optimize their investment.

publications.title: PAS As a Launchpad for Improved Customer Experience
publications.description: In order to meet the demands of customers and agents, carriers can benefit from moving from a policy-centric model and move to a customer-centric one. A modernized policy administration platform provides the necessary launch pad for carriers to offer a variety of highly differentiated customer experiences

headline: Global Data Quality Leader at PwC
about:
Arjun Vaikkam is an influential technology executive and empowering leader offering 20+ years of enterprise information architecture, data quality and governance, process improvement, strategic technology planning, team building, and project management expertise across the entertainment/media, pharmaceutical, healthcare insurance, and financial services industries.

Arjun is currently serving as the Global Data Quality Leader within the PwC's Global Chief Data Office. Data is a critical component to almost every initiative across the PwC network. As PwC's business is increasingly cross-border and because the brand is global, it is essential to leverage global technologies and establish common processes for measuring and evaluating the quality of the data for more effective risk, compliance and operational decisioning. When the PwC member firms (60+) operate in a similar manner, and utilise similar rules, processes and technologies, change can be created easily and quickly, and duplicated across the PwC network. Arjun is responsible for ensuring a standardised set of mechanisms exist to measure data quality and drive incremental improvements in collaboration with the data owners (e.g. member firms, global systems owners) across the Network. In addition, he is responsible for executing proactive and reactive measures around quality & governance including (1) the process reengineering required to set standards around how data is created and, maintained, (2) the transparency around the quality of data based on metrics and thresholds established and (3) the governance to define, manage and sustain the quality.

I am an Investigations & Forensics Partner in PwC’s Cyber, Risk & Regulatory practice, based in Dallas, TX. I regularly assist global companies doing business domestically, as well as throughout the globe.  I am a native Spanish speaker and have done extensive travel in Latin America, Europe and Asia leading combined US and local engagement teams on cross-border investigations, anti-corruption due diligence and compliance engagements. 
 
I work with legal, compliance and internal audit teams to lead domestic and international investigations including alleged asset misappropriation, financial frauds and corruption.  I also assist clients in responding to enforcement actions related to domestic and foreign bribery including FCPA, the Anti-Kickback Statute, Stark and False Claims Act among other regulations. I have also helped to represent clients and law firms in such matters, including the development of disgorgement calculations before the United States Department of Justice and the SEC.

I received a Bachelor of Business Administration (major in Finance and Spanish and  a concentration in International Business) from the University of Notre Dame, am a Certified Public Accountant (CPA), Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) and Certified in Financial Forensics (CFF). I am passionate about mentoring, diversity and inclusion and promoting women by co-leading the PwC Women's Inclusion Network and Parenting Inclusion Network in Dallas and serving as a board member of Step Up, a non-profit focused on mentoring teen girls.

about:
Lisa has been with PwC for over 28 years, beginning her career in client service before transitioning into Human Capital where she has held a variety of leadership positions before being named to her current role in 2021. Her experiences include performance and talent management, talent development, diversity & inclusion, total rewards and recognition, talent acquisition, partner affairs, coaching, employee engagement and operations. Lisa is able to design, implement and lead broad scope organization wide initiatives, while keeping a pulse on the practice. She is a strategic, trusted advisor with strong insight in aligning Human Capital with our business goals.

During her leadership tenure to date, PwC has been recognized for its achievements in human capital development and training, including being named to Fortune magazine's "100 Best Companies to Work For" and “50 Best Workplaces for Flexibility”, Diversity Inc.'s "Top 5," Working Mother's "Top 10," and Training Magazine's #1 ranking as an organization that excels at employee training and development. 

Lisa, her husband Mark, and their three children live in Elmhurst, IL. She loves tennis, yoga and enjoys coaching youth basketball.

publications.title: Swap Dealer Reporting: Onward and Upward
publications.description:
In this Our Take Special Edition, we examine the root causes of swaps reporting deficiencies,
summarize key changes resulting from the CFTC reporting rewrite, and outline actions swap dealers can
take to address both areas.

publications.title: Managing Strategic Transformations through a Readiness Framework
publications.description: In this paper, we examine how strategic middle- and back-office transformations can be managed through a “readiness” lens to better achieve a successful outcome and how an exit planning strategy can be leveraged if needed.

publications.title: Swap Dealer Compliance - Past and Future
publications.description:
It has now been over 10 years since Title VII of the Dodd-Frank Act (DFA) instituted sweeping reforms to increase transparency and accountability through swap dealer regulation. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) was given authority to oversee swaps while the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) was made responsible for security-based swaps. The industry has responded to new regulatory requirements from both agencies by developing compliance, risk management, reporting, and other processes and systems.
As regulatory conformance deadlines passed and swap dealer compliance matured, the CFTC and SEC began examining dealers and issuing enforcement actions. Over time, the severity of fines has increased – a trend that shows no sign of slowing down. This Our Take Special Edition discusses the evolution of swap dealer regulation and compliance over the last 10 years and considers what swap dealers can expect over the next 10 years.

publications.title: SEC Issues Risk Alert for Security-based Swap Dealer
publications.description:
On January 10th, the SEC issued a risk alert which highlights common deficiencies and
weaknesses in the compliance programs of security-based swap dealers (SBSDs) observed in examinations. This is the first public feedback from the SEC since examinations of SBSDs started in 2022.

publications.title: Communications Recordkeeping Fines Portend Further Scrutiny
publications.description:
The SEC and CFTC are closely scrutinizing broker-dealers, investment advisers and swap dealers’
practices around preserving and maintaining their employees’ “off-channel communications”
including messaging through text and encrypted applications. These firms are required to retain trade
information (e.g., daily trading records, data submitted to Swap Data Repositories) across formats
(e.g., electronic, oral communications) for the required duration (e.g., life of the trade plus five years
for electronic position records) in a manner that is identifiable, searchable, and retrievable.

publications.title: Derivatives: Year Ahead Roadmap
publications.description: It has been three years since the first wave of registrants applied to be swap dealers with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). Since then, dealers' compliance efforts have been challenged by lack of clarity in the rules and a multitude of CFTC no-action letters.

publications.title: Forging Consensus on TLAC
publications.description: On November 9, 2015, The Financial Stability Board (FSB) published its final standards on Total Loss Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) for Global Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs). The TLAC standards will require the world's 30 largest banks to finance themselves with a minimum amount of capital, and, for the first time, of long-term debt, such that the cost of their failure would be borne by investors rather than taxpayers.

slides.title: Quick Perspective on Agility and OKRs (objectives and key results)
slides.subtitle: Niket Desai on LinkedIn
slides.description: In this post our agile team put our heads together to share a quick perspective on Agile and OKRs. Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) is a goal setting system that encourages outcomes to be frequently set, tracked and re-evaluated. The concept, originated by Intel, was quickly adopted by other Silicon Valley companies, including Google. OKRs focus on outcomes rather than output. A proper goal describes what you want to achieve and how you are going to measure its achievement, the OKR framework simplified this and has two components: Objective - defines where you want to go. They are memorable qualitative descriptions of what you want to achieve. They should be short, inspirational and engaging and should motivate and challenge. Key Result(s) - set of metrics that measures your progress towards your objective. For each objective there should be 2 - 5 key results. OKRs and Agile Transformations At the highest level, an agile transformation is when a group of people say (and ideally exemplify) they want to move to more agile techniques and approaches for how they work with others - both inside and outside the four walls if you will. OKRs and agile transformations are hand in glove in that an Agile Transformation requires a strong vision of how the work processes will change in the future and in order for this to come to fruition, OKRs provide the way to measure it (and it's a common that we hear questions from our clients around this topic). If you are more interested in business agility and metrics you can read that article. Benefits At the core, OKRs help measure execution and outcomes (e.g. getting work done) versus expertise without execution (e.g.having only SMS knowledge) #SuccessfulAgileExecution. There are multiple benefits to this: 1 - #FocusedPriorities - OKRs force conversations around what is important and thus help reduce unnecessary churn around items that won’t help achieve the outcomes. Note, this assumes the organization knows how to prioritize and also knows how to manage “WIP” (work in progress). 2 - #MindsetShift - Appropriately defined OKRs across each level provides clarity and helps shift mindset to outcomes and associated behaviours (i.e., being Agile) vs gaming metrics (i.e., doing Agile) 3 - #Alignment - OKRs enable teams to align across all levels of the organization. Meaning, everyone knows the priorities and can self organize to achieve outcomes - this is illustrated in the graphic below. 4 - #Transparency - By setting OKRs across all levels of the organization (from CEO #AgileLeadership to Associate), it provides transparency, simplicity, and accountability to contribute to outcomes. 5 - #Crystal - OKRs are easy to understand and clear, even for folks that have limited knowledge of the product and thus helps them understand how they can contribute. To get more specific with some examples, please see the image below. This image shows a couple things, 1) where OKRs can tie into broader outcomes and pieces of work that should have measurable outcomes (in this illustration, classic agile units of work) 2) how OKRs and agile work ladders back up to the overall Corporate Goals (outcomes) so that anyone with OKRs understand how what they did for the personal OKRs benefits the organization as a whole. *note: the OKRs would be distinct at each of the levels above (i.e., one wouldn't use the same OKR to measure both a Corporate Goals and a Feature). Considerations: Simple & Clear: OKRs are valuable due to their simplicity in articulating what should be done; albeit, with inherent pitfalls that they can be written poorly Integrated into the Hierarchy: When scaling agile, OKRs have even more value when they tie to the hierarchy of how work is delivered (i.e., requirements), creating a conduit for clarity of “purpose” to teams and “feedback” to senior leadership (per the image above). Tooling: To get the most value, use tools that integrate well with each other / closely with your requirements. OKRs should be intimately tied to agile artifacts (e.g., epics, features, user stories), to ensure proper alignment/traceability to the objectives, as well as monitoring (via metrics) of whether we are getting closer to the objectives. It then follows that the tooling used to support OKRs should integrate seamlessly with the tooling for the agile artifacts (ideally, just one single tool). As an example consider this OKR: Objective: Reduce patient safety events in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) by 50% from last year Key Result 1: 75% reduction of medical dosing errors from last year Key Result 2: 50% reduction of ventilator-associated pneumonia from last year Key Result 3: 25% reduction of catheter-induced urinary infection from last year A potential epic (one of many) for the Key Result 1 may be: Epic: Utilize smart infusion pumps with dose-error reduction software (DERS) for intravenous applications integrated into the EHR A potential set of initial features for this epic (notice how they are iterative improvements upon MVPs): Feature 1: Acquire a smart pump with DERS and pilot usage Feature 2: Integrate DERS (smart pump drug library) into the EHR and align/standardize EHR to prevent misalignment with EHR orderable medications Feature 3: Develop computer based training for broader educational rollout to organization Each feature would be broken down into user stories, that as they are completed would drive the “progress bar” status for Key Result 1 This posting isn’t comprehensive in that it’d take more than a posting to cover more of the “how” around integrating OKRs and agile transformations. We hope this article provides enough context and perspective that one can clearly see the two are complementary. In addition to the “what”, we hope you have learned a bit about how these two can work together to achieve better results for your organization/team(s).

headline: IT Security and Compliance, Risk Management
about: Previously, leading SOC 1 & 2 engagements at Schellman equipped me with a robust understanding of the tech industry's compliance needs. My ability to collaborate effectively with clients on control creation and compliance management has been instrumental in navigating the complexities of regulatory requirements. With a steadfast commitment to excellence, my journey continues to be defined by a proactive stance in adapting to the ever-evolving landscape of IT security and compliance.

experience.position: Senior Associate - Risk & Regulatory IT Controls

experience.description:
● Led the fieldwork of SOC 1 & 2 engagements for clients in the tech industry. Controls include risk
management, network monitoring, and logical access.
● Collaborated with clients on appropriate control creation and compliance management.
● Conducted risk assessments for high-risk processing in connection with regulatory requirements, including data security, security breach notifications, and privacy by design

● Assisted GRC teams with assessment and documentation of compliance and risk posture as it relates to their IT infrastructure.
● Performed validation testing for ineffective controls remediated by clients within the finance industry.
● Initiated a procedure documentation project, outlining the steps necessary to communicate effectively with control owners and obtain appropriate evidence for multiple controls, including access management and change management.

●	Performed risk-based testing of controls for SOC 1 & 2 for clients within the healthcare industry. Controls tested includes logical/physical access, change management, monitoring, etc.
●	Acted as the internal IT auditor for clients preparing for ISO 27001 Certification. Controls tested includes HR Security, physical security, asset management, etc. 
●	Performed IT Risk Assessments of client applications, infrastructures, processes, and controls to provide management with an evaluation of IT related elements and their potential to impact the organization.
●	Led control and readiness walkthroughs with clients to gain an understanding of how their controls operate within their organization, as well as provide recommendations to enhance their overall IT environment.

●	Enrolled all physicians within a large health system in a multi-factor authentication application. Involved traveling to different hospitals in the surrounding area, introducing and teaching the doctors the new software being implemented.
●	Executed IT Audits for multiple clients within the insurance and oil/gas manufacturing industries. IT Controls tested included access management, change management, provisioning & deprovisioning, network intrusion detection, etc.

publications.title: CFPB fair lending: small business loans under review
publications.description:
Due to concerns that the credit needs of minority and women-owned small businesses are not being met, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) has prioritized small business lending as an area of focus for fair lending supervision this year. The CFPB’s fair lending examinations evaluate whether lenders exhibit patterns of discrimination based on a set of prohibited factors, such as race, ethnicity, or gender. 

On September 14th, the CFPB closed a Request for Information which was issued to help it better understand the small business lending market and explore opportunities for rulemaking. However, our experience indicates that the CFPB is not waiting on rulemaking and that fair lending supervisory reviews will become more frequent. As a result, lenders should review and enhance their small business fair lending practices and programs ahead of potential examinations.

This Regulatory Brief describes the CFPB’s expectations for small business fair lending and recommendations for lenders to manage compliance risks ahead of potential examinations.

publications.title: Expanding oversight: The CFPB’s new focus on service providers
publications.description:
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) recently announced that it would start directly supervising “large and key” service providers. This represents an expansion of the CFPB’s supervisory oversight because until now the CFPB has only reviewed service provider compliance as part of its examinations of financial institutions. Although this expansion of supervision does not come with any additional requirements for financial institutions, they should still consider potential impacts and review their relationships with key service providers.

The CFPB has already started conducting baseline reviews of certain service providers, along with targeted assessments of those in the mortgage lending market. Despite the dynamic political environment, service providers should not take a “wait and see” approach regarding the ongoing CFPB court case or potential actions by the Trump Administration to change the CFPB’s leadership as Director Richard Cordray has publicly stated that the CFPB intends to continue conducting examinations and enforcing existing rules.

This Regulatory brief describes the CFPB’s expectations for service providers’ compliance management systems and financial institutions’ service provider risk management programs, with recommendations for both to manage compliance risks ahead of examinations.

publications.title: Home Mortgage Disclosure Act: A sprint to the finish line
publications.description:
Beginning January 1st, 2018, mortgage lenders must begin collecting additional data in accordance with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s (CFPB) new Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) rule. While many lenders are making steady progress toward compliance with the new requirements, some lenders are taking a “wait and see” approach due to the uncertainty about the CFPB’s leadership and agenda and the Trump Administration’s regulatory review initiatives.

However, we do not expect to see significant revisions or a reversal of the CFPB’s rule. In fact, the CFPB recently issued its largest-ever fine for violating the existing HMDA requirements. As such, we expect examiners to not only continue to scrutinize reporting practices under the existing requirements, but also to monitor lenders’ progress with implementing the new requirements as part of their ongoing examinations.

publications.title: CFPB exams: Deposit accounts on the radar
publications.description:
As the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) continues to conduct examinations on banks’ deposit account practices, we expect to see a greater focus on the use of consumer reporting agencies (CRAs) to screen potential customers - an often overlooked aspect of these accounts. In addition to using CRA reports when deciding whether or not to open a new deposit account, banks are responsible for the accuracy of deposit account information reported to CRAs.

In recent years, banks have enhanced risk management oversight of credit reporting practices for loan accounts, but in our experience have yet to apply the same level of attention to deposit accounts. Accordingly, we recommend that banks proactively review their deposit account screening and reporting procedures to prepare for examinations.

This Regulatory brief describes the CFPB’s expectations for banks’ use of CRAs during deposit account administration and provides recommendations for banks to manage compliance risks ahead of examinations.

publications.title: Integrating compliance into financial technology initiatives
publications.description: Virtually every financial institution is enhancing or expanding its use of technology at a relentless pace to improve or automate existing infrastructure; to meet increasing customer demands; to support new products, services, access to information, or functionality to manage accounts; or to otherwise improve their business prospects. More broadly, the financial services industry is paying close attention to new technology companies offering innovative products and services designed to disrupt the market. Despite the many drivers for technology change, the financial services industry carries significant hurdles due to the complex supervisory environment and expectations for regulatory compliance.

headline: Director - Supply Chain Consulting at PwC
about:
Wuji has over 16 years of industry and consulting experience in developing and implementing transformational supply chain strategies across a range of industries.  He is passionate in helping companies realize EBITDA improvements through reshaping their supply chain strategies, redesigning business and operating models, improving operational performance, and transforming cost structures.  Wuji’s experience gives him a strong combination of breadth and depth in areas such as supply chain strategy, logistics network optimization, logistics strategy, supply chain operating model design, S&OP design and implementation, and supply chain technology.

Wuji holds an MBA from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business with a concentration in Strategy, Finance and Marketing.  He also has a Master’s degree from Case Western Reserve University with a concentration in Supply Chain Management. Wuji is certified by the Association for Operations Management (APICS) as a Certified Supply Chain Professional (CSCP).

experience.position: Head of Logistics Network Strategy - North America

experience.description:
Led 30+ supply chain strategy, capability building, cost reduction, and execution engagements to drive profitable growth across Hi-Tech and Industrial Products industries.
- Supply Chain Transformation (S&OP Focus) - Improved delivery performance by 60+ ppts. in 6 months through designing and implementing Supply Chain Transformation initiatives for an industrial OEM; segmented demand and drove forecast accuracy improvements by 10 ppts., established rough cut capacity planning and production scheduling capabilities in multiple factories, and identified 19% inventory optimization opportunities.
- Supply Chain Operating Model Design - Designed supply chain target operating model to support business growth for a telecom networking equipment OEM; identified $37M+ inventory improvement opportunity; guided Advanced Planning System implementation to support the target operating model.
- Logistics Network Optimization - Defined distribution network strategy to scale with global market expansion for a consumer electronics company; estimated 15% cost savings through product portfolio rationalization, distribution network and go-to-market channel optimization, and global tax/trade adjustments.
- Manufacturing Footprint Optimization and Site Selection - Optimized manufacturing footprint and distribution network to support 3-year strategic growth plan for an industrial OEM; recommended optimal facility footprint, manufacturing strategy, and CapEx investments.
- Strategic Sourcing - Led 3PL sourcing events for one of the largest consumer electronics companies to support e-commerce growth; developed 3PL strategy by identifying capabilities to keep in-house vs. outsource, defined warehouse automation capabilities to scale for peak seasons, launched RFQ and conducted vendor evaluations.
- Warehouse Operations Improvement - Improved warehouse inventory accuracy from 83% to 98%+ in 3 months by identifying root causes of fulfillment challenges; developed and executed warehouse playbook.

- Crafted customized supply chain solutions that generated new business revenue of more than $60M over 4 years:
- Identified, evaluated and prioritized key solution components that addressed clients’ needs.
- Developed models that assessed resource requirements; collaborated with operations to validate methodology.
- Prepared financial models and conducted sensitivity analysis that demonstrated change impact.
- Presented recommendations to clients’ senior management team; achieved close to 35% win rate.
- Secured the company’s first client with large scale technical service operations; expanded value-added service capabilities for future business growth and contributed $8M in revenue.
- Analyzed client’s transportation network and improved service level; identified over 12% saving opportunities and decreased time-to-market by 1 day in key regions; the solution was implemented in July 2012.
- Formulated and implemented a facility relocation strategy that reduced production cost and shrank inventory from 60 to 7 days; resulted in an annual savings of more than $2M.
- Improved customer satisfaction by increasing order fill rate by 20%; reorganized production process, balanced capacity and developed Standard Work Instructions that reduced production overtime by 15%.

- Gained advantage over competitions and hedged price increase risk by developing optimal purchasing recommendations; delivered more than $9M savings in 2 years.
- Led a team of 3 and introduced the first corporate-wide supplier scorecard that proactively managed suppliers’ performance; analyzed KPIs and explored tactics on price negotiation and supplier performance management.

headline: Senior Associate @ PwC | Technology Consulting
about:
2022 graduate of Georgia State University’s J. Mack Robinson College of Business. I am currently a Senior Associate in PwC’s Cloud Engineering, Data & Analytics advisory platform and serve as an advisor for our Chicago Community in Action Committee, providing strategic guidance to our five-person leadership team focused on delivering an array of volunteer opportunities to 4000 local staff while advancing the firm’s purpose and social responsibility goals.

My professional experiences have given me exposure and the opportunity to deliver value in the finance, healthcare, utility, retail, and transportation industries, as well as the non-profit sector. Skills include agile methodologies, business continuity management, brand strategy, business strategy, customer experience, data analysis & visualization, IT disaster recovery, product management, and project management. 

I have a passion for people & technology and seek opportunities where tech can be utilized to positively impact the lives of others. 

In my free time, I enjoy traveling, spending time with friends, volunteering, pursuing development opportunities, and trying new restaurants or recipes at home. I'm always open to travel and vegan recipe or restaurant recommendations, so feel free to send them my way!

Alongside a team of two core team members and one alternate team member, leveraged business case and market data to develop a strategy for strengthening P&G’s overall attractiveness as an employer of choice among top talent. 

Procter & Gamble (P&G), an American multinational consumer goods company is a “Master Brander” holding a portfolio of 65 unique brands in 10 different product categories including household names such as Tide, Bounty, Dawn, Mr. Clean, and NyQuil. With operations in 180 countries, P&G is a global leader leveraging its capabilities to deliver superior products and services while improving the lives of the world's consumers and their communities. 

With a renewed focus on leveraging their marketing capabilities to attract, develop, and retain highly competitive candidates, our team of consultants leveraged candidate data, a SWOT analysis, and our knowledge of current trends affecting the Millenial and Gen Z workforce, to deliver a strategy that would enhance P&G's employer-brand while promoting the inclusive, innovative, and inspiring work environment the company strives to deliver to its employees.

headline: From spreadsheets to soul work | PwC finance lead + yoga/breathwork guide
about:
I’m a Senior Finance Manager at PwC with over a decade of experience leading high-performing teams, streamlining operations, and solving complex problems with clarity and heart. But my journey doesn’t stop at spreadsheets.

I’m also the founder of Calibrē, a wellness brand devoted to bringing grounded, science-informed breathwork and nervous system tools into corporate and high-performance spaces. As a certified yoga instructor and breathwork facilitator-in-training, I’m passionate about creating calm in high-pressure environments and empowering people to reconnect to what matters.

I believe the corporate world and well-being don’t have to be at odds—they can (and should) coexist with intention. Whether I’m guiding a team through a system conversion or leading a breathwork session, my goal is the same: to foster clarity, connection, and resilience.

As a board member for No Shame On U, a nonprofit focused on eliminating the stigma around mental health, I’m deeply committed to shifting the conversation around emotional wellness—both personally and professionally.

If you’re building something at the intersection of business and well-being, I’d love to connect.

As I have interacted with my clients and industry peers I have learned the intricacies of managing complex international technology security considerations as well as industry specific challenges driven by law or by industry specific risks. Whether I am designing complex governance and compliance frameworks for Fortune 100 medical technology organizations,  leading cloud providers, or delivering controls based assessments focused on privacy and security (HIPAA, GAPP),  my clients tell me they  value my  insight and responsiveness as a trusted advisory to their organizations.

about:
I am a CPA with over 15 years of experience in federal, state, and local tax (SALT) compliance, tax consulting, and corporate tax strategy. My experience includes leadership roles at Deloitte and PwC, where I managed complex tax compliance engagements from the staff level, supported M&A due diligence, and advised clients across multiple industries on ASC 740 reporting, tax provision calculations, and multistate tax planning. I specialize in income and franchise tax compliance, unitary filings, apportionment analysis, audit defense, and state tax controversy. I’ve worked extensively on tax risk management, voluntary disclosure agreements (VDAs), and the implementation of tax technology platforms that support automation, workflow optimization, and regulatory reporting. My background also includes corporate, partnership and S corporation taxation, tax return review, and managing composite filings and quarterly estimates across jurisdictions.

I bring a process-driven mindset to tax department operations—improving data integrity, enhancing compliance readiness, and aligning internal controls with GAAP and regulatory standards. I’ve led cross-functional and geographically distributed teams, guided technical staff development, and managed client relationships in both advisory and compliance-driven environments. I’m passionate about improving the tax function through digital transformation, scalable process design, and strategic alignment with business goals. I’ve collaborated with corporate tax departments, accounting firms, and legal advisors on engagements ranging from tax compliance lifecycle management to transaction structuring and due diligence reviews.

headline: Senior Manager at PwC
about:
Strategic and results-driven financial services leader with over 13 years of experience advising Fortune 500 companies on regulatory compliance, operational risk, and technology enablement. I specialize in helping banks and insurers navigate complex regulatory landscapes while driving operational efficiency and cross-functional alignment.

Currently, I am a Senior Manager in Advisory Services at PwC where I’ve led and supported initiatives across major markets including New York, Chicago, and now Kansas City. My work spans regulatory strategy development, enterprise risk management, and program design for compliance readiness, for frameworks like Dodd-Frank, Federal Reserve Board and OCC standards, and the Department of Labor Fiduciary Rule.

I bring a strong foundation in financial planning and analysis, client relationship development, and project management. My background includes a JD from the University of Missouri School of Law and a B.S. in Business Administration with a focus in Finance, Banking, and Real Estate.

I’m passionate about leveraging technology, including platforms like Salesforce, Jira, and emerging AI tools like ChatGPT to streamline operations and enhance decision-making. I’ve had the opportunity to work across multiple markets, including New York, Chicago, and Kansas City, partnering with clients to solve challenges related to regulatory compliance, risk management, and operational transformation.  Examples of focused work includes managing regulatory reporting schedules and helping clients meet commitments to external regulators, often under frameworks like Dodd-Frank, FRB, and OCC guidelines, and NAIC model laws.

about:
As artificial intelligence reshapes the economy, I work at the intersection of technology, strategy, and equity to shape what comes next – and who gets to lead it. 

At PwC, I help financial institutions modernize how they operate and grow in a digital-first world. Whether it’s GenAI, cloud architecture, or next-gen platform design, I focus on what moves the work forward: clear strategy, aligned teams, measurable results.

My approach to leadership has always been rooted in equity. I help lead national efforts across PwC's Purpose & Inclusion strategy, from the Latino Inclusion Network to DEI innovation programs that challenge how we develop talent. That work is personal. Growing up in a family rooted in Chicago where opportunity felt uneven and inherited, I learned early that systems do not shift on their own. People shift them. Advocates shift them. Designers shift them. That belief shows up in how I lead inside and outside the firm, whether mentoring CPS students through Lumity, serving on advisory boards, or championing pathways for first generation and underrepresented leaders.

My work has been recognized by Yale SOM as an Emerging Leader in Innovation, by Hispanic Executive’s 30 Under 30 list, and through PwC’s Advisory MBA Scholar distinction. These milestones are meaningful, but the responsibility they represent matters more. They open doors to rooms where I now teach and speak, from tech conferences to university classrooms, helping others challenge systems, reframe narratives, and reimagine what leadership can look like next.

If you’re building what’s next in systems, leadership, or opportunity creation, I’m always up for the conversation.

publications.title: From Last Resort to First Movers: The Rise of Excess & Surplus (E&S) Insurance
publications.description: Once a marginal backstop for hard-to-place risks, the U.S. Excess and Surplus (E&S) market has become a $135 billion growth engine reshaping how insurers manage volatility and complexity. This whitepaper explores how rising catastrophe losses, cyber volatility, social inflation, and reinsurance tightening have propelled E&S from niche to mainstream. It shows how flexible underwriting, digital platforms, and AI-driven agility are transforming E&S into the industry’s laboratory for innovation and resilience.

publications.title: The Great Insurance Talent Cliff
publications.description: This piece challenges the perception of insurance as a fallback career and reframes it as one of the most overlooked accelerators for early-career leadership. With nearly half the P&C workforce set to retire by 2035, the industry faces a critical talent gap, yet few recognize the scale of opportunity within. From piloting AI tools to navigating climate and cyber risk, young professionals are stepping into high-impact roles not despite their age but because the industry urgently needs them. It’s a call to look beyond trendier sectors and see where real leadership, purpose, and upward mobility are being quietly redefined.

publications.title: Vision 2030: Transforming P&C Insurance with a Beyond Market Strategy
publications.description: The whitepaper highlights the critical role of public policy strategy in shaping the future of Property & Casualty (P&C) insurance, emphasizing the need for insurers to proactively engage with regulators, policymakers, and public opinion to influence legislative outcomes. By applying the Beyond Market Strategy (BMS) framework, insurers can help craft balanced regulatory policies that foster innovation, address emerging risks like climate change and cyber threats, and ensure fair AI-driven underwriting, positioning the industry as a collaborative partner in policy development rather than a passive respondent to regulatory changes.

publications.title: Bridging Analytics and Workflow: Transforming Underwriting with Integrated Desktop Platforms
publications.description: Our final PwC whitepaper as part of the "2025 Trends" Summer Reading series explores the rising adoption of underwriting desktop solutions by insurers to streamline workflows, enhance data-driven decision-making, and improve risk analysis. These platforms consolidate multiple core processes into a “single pane of glass,” providing underwriters with centralized access to workflows, data augmentation, and real-time analytics. With advanced geospatial tools and climate modeling via ESRI’s ArcGIS, these solutions empower insurers to address climate-related risk, optimize new business opportunities, and improve operational efficiency across underwriting processes.

publications.title: AI-Driven Document Management in Insurance
publications.description: Our PwC Insurance Transformation practice address insurers' challenges with document-heavy processes, particularly the manual handling of submission intake, bordereaux, and claims servicing documents. By leveraging AI-driven solutions like natural language processing (NLP) and optical character recognition (OCR), insurers can streamline these workflows, automate data extraction, and reduce reliance on high-maintenance robotic process automation. A case study highlights a successful implementation for a reinsurer, showcasing AI’s potential to automate and validate foreign-language bordereaux files, resulting in improved efficiency and reduced manual workload.

publications.title: Parametric Insurance: Redefining Claims and Risk with IoT
publications.description: Exploring the emerging role of parametric insurance products, which utilize a predefined "trigger" event to automate claim settlement, offers advantages like instant payouts, flexibility, and alignment with IoT data. While these policies streamline claims processes and reduce costs, they also present challenges such as the need for IoT infrastructure and pricing complexities due to basis risk. By leveraging a build-test-learn model, insurers can quickly implement parametric solutions, enabling them to capture new market opportunities, reduce claims expenses, and enhance customer risk management through data-driven insights.

publications.title: Minimum Viable Product for Insurance Transformation
publications.description: This whitepaper explores how insurers can leverage a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) approach to accelerate core transformation initiatives, emphasizing rapid, iterative releases for faster business impact. Unlike traditional Agile methods, MVP focuses on delivering a foundational set of capabilities in-market, allowing enhancements over a defined roadmap and fostering a “build-test-learn” culture. With an emphasis on minimal customization, streamlined documentation, and quarterly software increments, MVP enables insurers to achieve quicker go-lives, real-time feedback, and alignment with agile development principles.

publications.title: Trends in 2025: Platforms, Ecosystems & Embedded Insurance
publications.description: Our PwC Insurance experts examine five key trends shaping the future of insurance distribution, highlighting the role of platforms, ecosystems, and embedded insurance. It emphasizes how insurers are investing in both digital and embedded distribution models to meet shifting consumer preferences, accelerated by challenges from the COVID-19 pandemic. By leveraging composite API architectures, insurers can simplify partnerships and enhance distribution flexibility, paving the way for innovative and seamless purchasing experiences across traditional and alternative channels.

slides.title: CTRL+Think: Reclaiming Critical Thought Before It's Automated Away
slides.subtitle: Dan Segura on LinkedIn
slides.description: Introduction Artificial Intelligence (AI) is everywhere and for many rising professionals, that’s both exciting and disorienting. In most workplaces over the past year, many are being encouraged, if not outright expected, to embrace the AI revolution: use it to move faster, analyze smarter, and scale our work like never before. At plenty of well-known global consulting firms, there’s significant investment and momentum behind AI adoption. The message is clear: learn it, leverage it, lead with it. But once the workday ends, I shift into an entirely different mindset. As an MBA student at the Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Management, 6:00 PM CST signals a hard pivot, from delivering faster with AI, to slowing down and thinking more deeply without it; rooted in critical thinking, structured problem-solving, and navigating ambiguity. Here, the focus isn’t on how quickly you can generate a slide deck or automate a summary, but on how well you can challenge assumptions, think from first principles, and navigate ambiguity without shortcuts. Straddling these two worlds: the fast-evolving workplace and the traditional academic training ground, has made it clear that finding balance is one of the most important and difficult challenges for the next generation of business leaders. How do we lean into the power of AI without letting it dull the very skills we’re supposed to be sharpening? How do we remain analytical, thoughtful professionals while taking advantage of tools that promise to “think” for us? In this op-ed-style piece, I’ll share a personal lens on that tension and explore how younger professionals, especially those early in their management careers, can use AI to enhance their work without sacrificing the development of their own strategic judgment. We’ll break down where AI helps, where it hinders, and how to find balance between speed and substance. The goal isn’t to resist AI, but to use it with intention so we don’t lose the mental edge that sets great thinkers and leaders apart. And to quote one of my favorite short series, The Vince Staples Show: "This is a work of fiction. Any similarities to actual events are purely coincidental. (Except they’re not.)" The “Promise” of AI: Efficiency, Insight, and Career Growth We’ve all heard the promises loud and clear: AI will supercharge productivity, eliminate busywork, and unlock unprecedented speed and scale in how we work. And in many workplace settings. including consulting, those promises are already being realized. I’ve seen firsthand how generative AI tools can reduce research time, accelerate document creation, and streamline data analysis. In theory and in practice, this has allowed individuals and teams to shift from doing to thinking, automating the tactical so we can focus on the strategic. Whether it’s writing a proposal draft, synthesizing a dataset, or prepping for a client workshop, AI can act as a time-saving co-pilot. The efficiency is real. But so is the creeping concern: If AI becomes the default starting point, how long until it also becomes the endpoint, replacing not just task execution but the thinking behind it? That’s where caution [and humility] must come in. AI doesn’t “know” anything; it predicts based on patterns. Numerous studies have documented algorithmic bias, data hallucinations, and factual inaccuracies. While AI can be a great accelerant, it doesn’t yet offer context, discernment, or ethical nuance. If we begin to blindly trust AI outputs without questioning the data behind them or the logic beneath them, we risk weakening the very skills we’re trying to strengthen like judgment, reasoning, and synthesis. And that’s a subtle but slippery slope. It’s easy to accept AI-generated answers at face value, especially when they’re framed well. But easy answers can be shallow ones; and real leadership demands depth. At the same time, we shouldn’t ignore what AI unlocks, especially for those of us early in our careers. AI tools allow us to step into conversations and roles that previously required deep subject matter expertise. By reducing dependency on niche technical knowledge, they help younger professionals operate with more breadth. I’ve used AI to model market entry scenarios, draft summaries of technical reports, and pressure-test ideas across functional domains I otherwise wouldn’t touch. In short, AI can fill gaps not with perfect knowledge, but with good enough scaffolding to help us contribute, ask better questions, and grow faster. This capability can be career-changing. It levels the playing field and provides a sense of confidence and autonomy. When used intentionally, it enables you to show up to meetings more prepared, make smarter recommendations, and learn through iteration. Instead of waiting for subject matter experts or spending hours on foundational research, AI lets you build from a higher starting point. Still, the constant push to integrate AI can feel overwhelming. There’s a pressure to always be faster, more optimized, and more plugged in. The hype is everywhere! Executives promoting adoption, companies racing to build AI into workflows, and peers touting how they used AI to 10x their productivity. It’s easy to feel like you’re behind if you’re not fully onboard. But the right mindset is balance. Optimism, tempered by skepticism. Adoption, tempered by reflection. The best way forward is not to resist AI or worship it; it’s to partner with it. Let it handle the mechanical, help with the messy, and challenge you to think differently. But never let it replace your critical thinking. Because in a world where AI can produce answers in seconds, the real value lies in knowing which questions to ask, and why. The Risks: Outsourcing Our Intuition Despite AI's substantial benefits, its increased use can unintentionally erode essential critical thinking skills. Recent studies by Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon suggest professionals heavily relying on AI tools may experience diminished independent analytical capabilities. The convenience of AI-driven solutions can lead younger managers to accept generated outcomes without rigorous scrutiny, potentially creating blind spots in decision-making. This issue becomes even more relevant for those in MBA programs or leadership development tracks. These experiences are designed to help professionals learn how to diagnose complex problems, challenge assumptions, and make tough calls with incomplete information. If AI does the heavy lifting, it’s easy to fall into the habit of verifying output instead of generating it from scratch. And that mental habit of going through the reps, of building your strategic “muscle" isn’t one you want to lose early in your career. Overreliances on AI can also reinforce existing biases and create informational echo chambers. AI models trained on historical data often reproduce the assumptions and blind spots embedded in that data. As a result, using AI to guide strategy without human oversight could mean replicating outdated thinking, missing edge-case risks, or ignoring emerging trends. For a generation of professionals trying to drive innovation and break new ground, that’s a serious concern. Furthermore, psychological research suggests that frequent reliance on digital tools can lead to “cognitive offloading” where individuals delegate not just tasks but thinking itself to machines. Over time, this can diminish one's ability to synthesize information or draw independent conclusions. For rising professionals in strategic roles, this is particularly risky. Strategic leadership is not about retrieving the right answer, but truly about framing the right question, often in ambiguous contexts with no clear path forward. There’s also a more subtle risk: loss of ownership. When the tool produces the strategy, the memo, or the analysis, it can be harder to fully own the outcome. You may find yourself defending a position you didn’t fully think through, or implementing a plan you didn’t truly shape. And over time, this passive posture can lead to disengagement or worse, dependency. Willie the Wildcat, Northwestern's mascot, stands at the intersection of Ctrl and Think - A visual metaphor for every MBA trying to balance AI efficiency with strategic depth. (Fittingly, illustrated by generative AI) The Personal Balancing Act: Using AI Without Losing Yourself To maximize AI’s benefits without sacrificing critical thinking, rising professionals and managers should treat AI as a partner, not a crutch. That means using it to supplement your thinking, not substitute it. Here are a few guiding principles I’ve picked up as both a consultant and an MBA student: Begin with Curiosity, Not Convenience: Start by developing your own point of view before asking AI for assistance. Sketch a rough hypothesis, outline your assumptions, or build a quick framework. Then use AI to test and refine, not replace, that thinking. When we start with our own ideas, AI becomes a collaborator rather than a shortcut. This habit reinforces independent judgment and helps you build strategic instincts over time. In fast-paced environments, it’s tempting to default to whatever’s easiest, but real growth comes from mental reps, not just mechanical execution. Treat AI Like a Smart but Inexperienced Analyst: AI can deliver fast, well-formatted outputs, but it lacks context, judgment, and often, accuracy. Think of it like a junior team member: helpful, fast, sometimes brilliant, but not infallible. Interrogate its results. Ask: What data is this based on? What’s missing? Would I make this decision without AI’s input? When we challenge AI’s answers the way we would challenge any recommendation, we maintain accountability for the final judgment. This mindset keeps humans in the loop as decision-makers, not just editors. Use Time Saved to Go Deeper, Not Shallower: AI can save hours on execution, but what you do with that time is what matters. Don’t let efficiency become complacency. Reinvest that saved time into more thorough analysis, stakeholder conversations, creative ideation, or simply reflecting more deeply on the strategy. Use AI to accelerate routine work so you can slow down for the things that matter most. Strategic thinking isn’t just about solving problems, it’s about framing them, exploring them, and having the judgment to ask better questions before rushing to answers. For companies, the takeaway is this: don’t just teach your junior talent to use AI tools - teach them when not to. Build cultures where questioning, skepticism, and deep analysis are rewarded. And for MBA programs, continue emphasizing case studies, Socratic discussion, and real-world ambiguity. That kind of environment is more valuable and critical than ever. Conclusion: The Thinking That Still Sets Us Apart In the workplace, AI can feel like a superpower; accelerating analysis, removing roadblocks, and producing polished outputs in record time. In the classroom, we’re reminded of a different truth: that the best decisions start not with answers, but with better questions. Rather than seeing these two worlds as contradictory, we must see them as complementary. The future belongs to professionals who can toggle between both modes: (1) those who can harness technology for speed and scale, but (2) also pause, reflect, and think deeply when it matters most. AI isn’t going anywhere, and that’s a good thing. It offers immense potential to unlock creativity, democratize access to information, and help us reach new levels of productivity. But it also demands something greater from us: intention. The professionals who will lead the next generation of business aren’t the ones who simply use AI the most. They’re the ones who use it best: with discernment, with discipline, and with a clear understanding of its strengths and its limits. We are the first generation of professionals with AI in the workplace by our side. That means we carry both opportunity and responsibility. We have the chance to shape how this technology is adopted, how it influences culture, and how it elevates or erodes our thinking. The playbook isn’t written yet. We get to write it. Let’s make it a manual for using AI not to replace human thought, but to sharpen it. Let’s use AI to do more, and think harder. So as you step into your next team meeting, project, or strategic challenge, pause and ask yourself: "Am I using this tool to enhance my judgment, or avoid exercising it?" The answer will define more than just your next task. It may define the kind of leader you become. Because at the end of the day, your most valuable asset isn’t the smartest tool in your tech stack ..... it’s the way you think! Or, to bring it full circle and with a nod to The Vince Staples Show: "Sometimes it takes a little fiction to get us to confront the truth. What’s exaggerated on screen isn’t far off from what we’re grappling with in real life." A world that’s changing fast, where smart tools are everywhere, but smart thinking still sets you apart. From a former high school newspaper writer turned consultant + MBA student - This piece was both personal and a blast to write. Thanks for reading! publications.description: Oceanic exploration has become an emerging field of research due to many resources located in the deep sea. Development of underwater Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs) is an important area of research. This paper describes a simple ROV prototype based on low cost boards, Raspberry Pi and Arduino UNO. The ROV has been tested for the above basic operations.

headline: Corporate Attorney, In-House Counsel & Legal Advisor | Global Contracts, Transactions & Governance | Director, OGC at PwC | Translating business goals into practical legal solutions with responsible AI enhanced workflows
about:
I’m a corporate generalist attorney with more than a decade of experience structuring complex transactions and counseling U.S. and international companies on contracts, governance, and compliance. After earning my JD with honors from a top-ranked law school, I spent seven years at a global law firm advising multinational businesses and financial institutions on structured finance transactions and regulatory compliance. For the past four years, I’ve worked in-house, partnering with teams across Professional Services, Treasury, Real Estate, and more to craft practical legal solutions.

At the law firm, I gained expertise structuring intricate deals and navigating regulatory regimes. Today, I bring the same analytical approach in-house, helping organizations operate securely and efficiently. I also work on legal AI adoption — identifying use cases to streamline workflows while safeguarding confidentiality, data security and quality.

I bring technical precision and a collaborative, approachable style to every matter. My strength is translating business terms into contracts and policies that preserve key protections without undermining strategic goals. Whether negotiating borrower-side financings, drafting international services contracts, or advising on governance and compliance, I balance detail with pragmatism.

Here’s a little more about me outside of work (if you're curious):
➤ Girl Mom of Three. A trio of budding artists, ballerinas, and afternoon-tea enthusiasts keeps me on my toes.
➤ Travel Enthusiast. I booked my daughters’ passport appointments before they could roll over, and crafting detailed itineraries (with backup plans to the backup plans) is my love language.
➤ Oboist. I performed with the Charlottesville Symphony Orchestra, and a milestone was playing in the pit for a production of Les Misérables.
➤ Classics Nerd. I'm perpetually drawn to Ovid, Homer, and Catullus and never tire of mythology-inspired retellings.
➤ Cat Lady. Every Zoom call is better with a feline cameo.
➤ Avid Fiction Reader. I devour fantasy and sci-fi series and inevitably get too attached to fictional characters.
➤ Amateur Ballroom Dancer. I once performed a cha-cha showcase while 39 weeks pregnant.
➤ Peloton Loyalist. My “me time” is my 5 A.M. ride, yoga flow, or strength session before the rest of the house wakes up.
➤ Swiftie. I’m raising the next generation of feminist fans, one set of millennial-style heart hands at a time.

At work and at home, I’m relatable and empathetic — but in lawyering, I’m determined, strategic, and unwavering in protecting my clients.

publications.title: Realizing the Best of Both Worlds: An Engaged Workforce and More Satisfied Citizens
publications.description:
A local government’s staff deliver the day-to-day services that provide for the health, safety, and welfare of the community. Employee engagement is the degree to which an employee is passionate about and committed to their job and organization. If staff are fully engaged in their jobs, then they will put in the extra effort needed to provide the best services possible. If they are disengaged they will, at best, put in the bare minimum effort necessary to satisfy their job description and, at worst, will actively seek to undermine the organization.

The difference in work quality for engaged and disengaged employees is not trivial. One study found the following differences between work units in the top quartile in employee engagement versus work units in the bottom quartile:

    17% greater productivity
    41% less absenteeism
    10% higher customer satisfaction
    40% fewer defects in work products

 this report, we will show you how local governments can improve employee engagement, thereby improving productivity and reducing turnover. More importantly, we’ll show how to make a difference in the lives of staff members like Maria and, thereby, make a difference in how your local government serves its community. The first part of this report is about getting the right people in the job. If the job is a good match to the person to start with, it will be easier to engage them. Second, we will address how to engage employees after they are hired. Here, we will show how the culture of the organization can be shaped to encourage engagement and managerial tactics that can be used to bolster engagement.

headline: Retired PwC Deals Principal
about:
I retired from PwC on June 30, 2023.  Prior to my retirement, as a PwC Deals Principal, I focused on the valuation of businesses, intangible assets, as well as equity and debt securities for financial and tax reporting.  With my seasoned background in finance and valuation, I’ve helped clients with:
* multinational valuation analyses for tax and general corporate planning
* purchase price allocations for both financial reporting and tax
* negotiating and executing mergers, acquisitions and joint ventures for buy-side and sell-side  
* financial and economic analyses in consumer, industrial products sectors

I brought to PwC more than 30 years of corporate finance experience and over twenty-five years of valuation experience. Before rejoining PwC in 2010, I served as a Managing Director in Houlihan Lokey's Chicago office where I provided financial valuation services to a wide range of clients and was responsible for the Tax and Financial Reporting Valuation practice in the Midwest Region. 

Prior to my eight years at Houlihan Lokey, I served as a senior manager in the Strategic Valuation Services practice in Arthur Andersen's Chicago office and as a director in the Corporate Value Consulting practice at PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP. 

Throughout my career, I have focused on serving clients in the consumer and industrial products sectors and have extensive experience performing financial and economic analyses of operating businesses across a wide variety of industries. 

I graduated from Cornell University, majoring in economics earning "with distinction" in all subjects. I then went on to receive an MBA in finance, marketing, and accounting, "with distinction," from the J.L. Kellogg Graduate School of Management, Northwestern University. I currently hold the designation of Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) and am a member of the Association for Investment Management & Research and the Investment Analysts Society of Chicago.

volunteering.description:
The mission of the Daniel Murphy Scholarship Fund (DMSF) is to give high school scholarship assistance and educational support to Chicago students from economically disadvantaged backgrounds. DMSF seeks to make a life-altering difference in the lives of its Scholars by providing them with the best opportunity to succeed in high school and college.  DMSF conducts five “Core Programs” designed to enhance the lives of its scholars.  Those programs begin during the summer before new Scholars enter high school, and continue through the college admission process. 
1) Bridge to Excellence Program: 
Intensive week-long workshop focusing on the academic and business language that is expected of them in the college preparatory environment.  
2) Tutoring: 
Professional tutors provide academic assistance to Scholars who need extra help throughout their high school careers.
3) Mentoring and Affinity Group Programs: 
Matched with an adult who serves as a role model with a special interest in the academic success and personal growth of the Scholar.  DMSF also facilitates affinity groups that meet twice a month. 
4) Summer Opportunities Fair 
Access to summer job opportunities, internships, study abroad programs, and community service programs.  DMSF also supports summer golf caddie employment opportunities.  Scholars live in college dorms and caddie at nearby country clubs, earning income, gaining work experience and developing life skills.  Participating in the Caddie Program makes Scholars eligible to apply for the Chick Evans Scholarship, a four-year, full tuition college scholarship awarded by the Western Golf Association.  Approximately 200 DMSF Scholars who have participated in the Caddie Program have been awarded an Evans Scholarship. 
5) College Counseling: 
Assists Scholars and their families with all aspects of the college selection and application process

I worked in a team with a perinatal pathologist, OBGYN, and epidemiology PhD fellow in the Department of Anatomic Pathology at NorthShore's Evanston Hospital. I supported 3 research projects: 1.) an examination of trimester of COVID infection and placental pathology outcomes; 2.) the effect of placental share of twins on placental pathology; and 3.) inter-observer agreement on placental pathology diagnoses between an expert perinatal pathologist vs general pathologists. With these projects, I analyzed over 1,000 placental pathology reports, extracted relevant information from them, and conducted data analysis via Microsoft Excel and Access to identify significant insights related to each project's research question. For the project on inter-observer agreement on placental pathology, I composed the initial draft of the research paper. The abstract of this paper, for which I am identified as the second author, was selected for presentation at the Society for Pediatric Pathology Fall 2022 Meeting.

I worked as an intern for the Golby Lab (Image Guided Neurosurgery Lab), which is a part of the Brigham and Women's Hospital in Cambridge. During this remote internship, I analyzed preoperative and intraoperative brain scans and segmented the cortical vessels using a software called 3DSlicer. I met weekly with my supervisor to discuss my progress and better understand the implications of my work in the subsequent phase of the project. The 3D segmentations I produced were used in the development of a Python-based deep learning approach to automatically classify cortical vessels from brain scans.

headline: Campus Talent Acquisition Manager at PwC
about:
A Message to Candidates:

Hi Candidates! 
I am so grateful that you are considering applying for opportunities at PwC! In an effort to be respectful of your time and inMail credits, I want to answer a few FAQs. I will serve as your direct point of contact if you attend one of the following universities: Florida State University, Florida International University, University of Miami, and University of North Florida

Q: I am interested in internship opportunities at PwC. Can you tell me about your Winter/Summer internship opportunities?
A:  For more information on our openings, check out our entry-level jobs site: https://jobs.us.pwc.com/entry-level. We typically hire a one to two years out, so it is never too early to start the job search! I recruit for our Audit, Tax, and Digital Assurance & Transparency roles. 

Q: I am an Accounting student and will be graduating this year with my 150 credit hours and am interested in full-time opportunities at PwC. Can you tell me about your openings?
A: Early congratulations! Check out our Entry-Level Associate opportunities on the website shared in my last answer. While we are hiring for many positions, I focus on Audit, Tax, and Digital Assurance & Transparency. If you applied for one of these programs, I'm happy to answer questions about these programs. 

Q: I recently graduated, and I am looking for full-time opportunities. 
A: Congratulations! At PwC, we determined what type of recruiting you do based on your graduation date. If you are in school or graduated within the past year, you are considered an entry-level recruit. If you have graduated over one year ago, you are considered an experienced-level recruit. Experienced positions allow you to apply and be hired immediately compared to entry-level positions that require a future start date months in advance. Please visit our Experienced Recruiting Page to learn more: https://jobs.us.pwc.com/

Connecting with recruiters on LinkedIn is tricky. Hopefully this made it a little easier!

headline: Director, Delivering Deal Value (DDV) at PwC
about:
I build growth at the intersection of deals, people, and technology.

I’m a Director focused on TMT transactions and large-scale transformations, where value is created (or lost) early — in integration strategy, operating model design, and how leaders mobilize their people. I enter deals upstream, when people risk and value first become visible, and turn those insights into expanded commercial scope and repeatable, AI-enabled delivery.

My work spans HR IMO, integration strategy, workforce transformation, and value creation — with a consistent focus on measurable outcomes.

What differentiates me:
	•	I connect deal strategy to execution, not theory
	•	I translate human capital insight into enterprise value
	•	I lead through complexity, aligning leaders, teams, and technology during moments of change

AI-driven disruption, regulatory pressure, and operating model shifts are accelerating deal activity — especially in TMT. I help clients move faster, integrate smarter, and realize value sooner by putting people at the center of the transaction.

I graduated cum laude from DePaul University in June, 2008 with a BSC in Accounting and Management.

headline: Tax Principal, PwC National Tax Services - International Tax Services

location.linkedinText: Washington, District of Columbia, United States

about:
Tax principal and member of PwC’s Washington National Tax practice, based in Washington DC, where I was the Leader of International Tax from 2012-2023.  I have experience advising clients in all aspects of international taxation, with a particular focus on international mergers, acquisitions and restructurings and the US anti-deferral rules. I also work closely with US and non-US based multinationals on cross-border financing, cash redeployment and other planning issues.

Before PwC, I served as a senior executive in the US Treasury Department where I worked for the Office of Chief Counsel, Internal Revenue Service as the Deputy Associate Chief Counsel (International – Technical). In that capacity, I had primary responsibility for the oversight of published guidance related to the taxation of cross-border investment and related issues. 

I also held positions as a partner in the Tax Department of McDermott Will & Emery LLP in Chicago, Illinois, serving as an international tax attorney for large US and non-US multinational corporations. Other work experience also includes the Washington National Tax Office of Deloitte and the Washington DC office of Weil Gotshal & Manges LLP.

I served on the Board of International Tax Advisors and as a guest lecturer for New York University School of Law’s graduate tax program. Additionally, I served on the Board of Visitors for the University of Montana School of Law, and as a longtime Vice-Chair of the ABA’s Foreign Activities of US Taxpayers committee, and as Chair of the DC Bar’s New Tax Practitioners subcommittee.

I have authored numerous articles on cross-border tax issues and am a frequent speaker on such issues, and serve on the Board or as chairman for various tax conferences, including The University of Chicago Federal Tax Conference, PLI’s International Tax Conferences and GWU-IRS’s International Tax Conference.
